title: Database connection pooling
summary: Sizing, lifecycle, and pitfalls of database connection pools for our Postgres workloads.

content.overview: A connection pool keeps a bounded set of open database connections so that requests do not pay the TCP+TLS+auth handshake on every query. Right-sizing the pool is more important than raising the max — Postgres performs best with a small number of busy connections.
content.details: Rule of thumb for Postgres: pool size = ((core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count) per app instance, capped well below max_connections. Use a connection-level timeout (e.g., 5s) and an acquisition timeout (e.g., 1s) so clients fail fast under load instead of queueing forever. Health-check connections cheaply (SELECT 1) before issuing user queries, and recycle connections older than ~30 minutes to handle network/firewall idle drops.
content.examples: asyncpg pool: asyncpg.create_pool(dsn, min_size=5, max_size=20, max_inactive_connection_lifetime=1800). HikariCP: maximumPoolSize=20, connectionTimeout=1000, idleTimeout=600000, maxLifetime=1800000.
content.caveats: A single oversized pool per app times many app instances equals thundering herd on Postgres. Consider PgBouncer in transaction mode in front of Postgres if you must scale instances. Long-running transactions hold a pool slot — never start a transaction before doing slow external I/O.
